title: Uncovering Latent Bias in LLM-Based Emergency Department Triage Through Proxy Variables

bias_targets.methodology: Evaluating shifts in LLM-predicted Emergency Severity Index (ESI) scores when inserting positive versus negative proxy variable qualifiers related to social determinants (e.g., median income, insurance status, health literacy, area deprivation, employment type) into standardized patient triage scenarios.

Analyzing how the LLM's polarity-dependent reactions to certain proxy variables (e.g., arrival by ambulance) create accidental racial disparities in triage acuity predictions, driven by underlying population-level differences in proxy distribution between White and Black patients.
Measuring changes in predicted ESI scores when patient scenarios are modified with proxy qualifiers indicating mental health history, substance use, and recent justice system involvement.
Assessing the shift in model-assigned ESI acuity scores based on patient clinical history qualifiers, such as continuity of care, prior ED visits, and access to a primary care provider.
Comparing model ESI predictions for patients described as speaking English fluently versus those described as having limited English proficiency and requiring an interpreter.

Testing the LLM's triage predictions against contextual environmental and logistical factors like ED crowding, arrival time, seasonal factors, and provider shift changes, which should not dictate clinical acuity.
